rv.q: Perfect, then, as anticipated, for the summer and the school-holidays but, more unexpectedly, for these jittery, fear-filled times too; a potent juvenile rallying cry to resist hard-knocks and fight back.
Its mixture of open-heartedness, wit and pizzazz enables the little orphan inside us all to see off our enemies.
And its Hart is definitely in the right place.
Nikolai Foster's production is smart, vivacious and boasts eye-catching casting in the shape of television favourite Miranda Hart as the gin-guzzling orphanage boss, Miss Hannigan.
But ‘Annie’ has its own charms, and though I suspect this production may not survive Hart’s departure on September 17, there is definitely more to it than celebrity casting.
Her singing is really remarkably bad: a coyote yowl, no more in key than a crane swinging in a high breeze.
But Hart is this revival’s selling point and I feel decidedly ambivalent about her performance.
Its message is both humane and inspiring and, in song after catchy song, hammered home.
The West End has another welcome hit.
If that sounds like you, book now, you'll have a great time too.
Instead, what we get is a game if rather reined-in performance that allies her foghorn of a singing voice to some signature physical comedy, not least the brief horse's canter at the curtain call.

The balance between the sweetness of Charles Strouse and Martin Charnin’s hugely popular score and the darker social issues is handled with a canny touch: ragged costumes proclaim injustice but the jazz-hands magic wins out.
Matilda may have lit a fire under this creative team, but Annie , all by herself, remains a soothing, celebratory treat.
The surprise here is that there is less fluff and more social realism to this Broadway classic of 1976 than its reputation suggests.

cn.t: This feel-good revival delivers timely optimism with slick staging and spirited performances, though critics note Miranda Hart's West End debut lacks menace and the show pales beside Matilda's wit.
